**Abstract**  
Using off-the-shelf generative large language models (LLMs) to simulate human respondents (silicon sampling) severely biases downstream econometric inference, while standard fine-tuning requires individual choice microdata that most published studies never release.
We align single-pass decision models that output normalized choice probabilities directly over valid options without text generation, making linear regression estimators directly differentiable in model weights.
To unlock studies that report only experimental designs and aggregate regression tables, we derive an unbiased mini-batch population-$\boldsymbol{\beta}$ loss that pairs a frozen base-probability control variate with split-sample cross-products, stabilized by a Kullback-Leibler anchor on table-only data or respondent-level cross-entropy (CE) on available microdata.
We evaluate open-weight decision models across five data-access regimes trained on consumer delivery and electricity-plan choice studies and tested zero-shot on an airline conjoint experiment and a six-arm nutrition-labeling randomized trial.
Microdata CE fine-tuning substantially lowers out-of-sample treatment-effect mean squared error (MSE), table-only training beats the off-the-shelf baseline without a single respondent choice, and hybrid microdata-plus-table training transfers missing price and green-energy trade-offs to close [TBD]% to [TBD]% of the gap toward a full-microdata oracle.


**Keywords.** Decision models, Silicon sampling, Econometric inference, Conjoint analysis, Marketing research


# Introduction {#sec-intro}

Simulating consumer choices, attitudes, and survey responses with foundation models, commonly referred to as silicon sampling, has attracted growing interest in marketing and behavioral research.
In marketing research, the primary goal is downstream econometric inference, such as estimating attribute slopes in conjoint analysis or causal treatment effects in randomized experiments.
Currently, research relies on off-the-shelf generative large language models (LLMs) that generate text autoregressively.
However, replacing human respondents with off-the-shelf generative LLM outputs severely biases downstream regressions because post-training for deterministic reasoning and safety compliance collapses choice uncertainty and triggers safety refusals on sensitive options [@goli2024frontiers; @leng2026reducing; @wang2026large].
Whereas existing post-inference methods adjust or reweight fixed model outputs using target-study human data [@leng2026reducing; @wang2026large], we align models before inference through their output architecture and training supervision.

Architecturally, we adopt single-pass decision models [@palmer2026kev].
Instead of generating text tokens, a decision model takes a respondent persona and a structured choice task and outputs a normalized probability distribution over the valid options in one forward pass.
This readout eliminates sampling variance and safety refusals while making linear regression estimators, such as ordinary least squares (OLS), directly differentiable in the model weights.
Yet architecture alone is insufficient because off-the-shelf decision models are pretrained on single-label objective benchmarks, treating disagreement among respondents who share a persona as classification error and biasing regression estimates.
Minimizing cross-entropy (CE) on individual choice microdata resolves this miscalibration when respondent choices are observed.
In practice, however, raw choice microdata is scarce, proprietary, or privacy-restricted, whereas thousands of published marketing studies release only experimental designs and aggregate regression tables.

Training a decision model directly on published regression coefficients $\boldsymbol{\beta}^*$ via mini-batch gradient descent presents two statistical challenges.
First, population OLS slopes depend on choice probabilities across all tasks in a study rather than one mini-batch; fitting OLS within small batches chases finite-sample noise, whereas squaring a single-batch estimate of the population slopes introduces variance bias that penalizes persona heterogeneity.
Second, matching a small vector of aggregate slopes leaves individual choice entropy unconstrained, allowing predicted probabilities to drift toward zero or one.
We address the first challenge with an unbiased population-$\boldsymbol{\beta}$ loss that uses frozen base-model probabilities as a control variate and multiplies estimation errors across two disjoint half-batches without using respondent choices.
We address the second challenge by pairing this loss with an entropy anchor, using Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence toward base probabilities for table-only training or respondent-level CE on available microdata for hybrid training.

We evaluate this framework across a five-regime data-access ladder using open-weight decision models [@palmer2026kev] trained on a US drone-delivery discrete-choice experiment [@berke2023drone] and an electricity-plan conjoint study [@wu2025partisan], and evaluated zero-shot on an unseen sustainable-aviation-fuel flight conjoint [@goldfarb2026comfort] and a six-arm nutrition-labeling randomized trial [@grummon2025nutrition].
Our design establishes three contributions.
First, CE fine-tuning on respondent microdata substantially lowers zero-shot treatment-effect mean squared error (MSE) on unseen experiments relative to the off-the-shelf model, whether training on single-study delivery microdata or on full microdata across both studies as an upper-bound oracle.
Second, without access to respondent choices, training solely on the eight published electricity slopes of @wu2025partisan improves out-of-sample MSE over the off-the-shelf baseline, and combining those published slopes with @berke2023drone delivery microdata transfers household price and green-energy trade-offs that delivery microdata alone lacks.
Third, progressing from table-only to hybrid training closes [TBD]% to [TBD]% of the out-of-sample MSE gap toward the unattainable full-microdata oracle.

# Literature review {#sec-lit}

Early work in silicon sampling prompted generative LLMs with demographic profiles to simulate human responses in political, economic, and marketing surveys [@argyle2023out; @horton2023large; @brand2023using; @goli2024frontiers; @sarstedt2024using; @pmlr-v202-santurkar23a; @durmus2024towards].
Although generative LLMs often capture the direction of average preferences, prior studies document systematic discrepancies from human populations, including mode collapse onto a single option, attenuated within-group variance, demographic stereotyping, and prompt sensitivity [@pmlr-v202-santurkar23a; @shu-etal-2024-dont; @koo2024benchmarking; @kabir-etal-2025-break; @deas-mckeown-2025-artificial; @jung-etal-2026-psychometric; @wadi2025monte; @zahradnickova2026ai].
In marketing applications, these distortions severely bias downstream econometric estimation [@goli2024frontiers; @leng2026reducing; @wang2026large].
In choice-based conjoint analysis, relying on simulated choices or naively pooling them with human data biases preference estimates, while scaling model capability or chain-of-thought reasoning worsens error by inducing overly deterministic choices [@wang2026large].
Recent marketing studies address these discrepancies after inference by treating the language model as a fixed generator, using target-study human benchmark data to statistically debias downstream regression parameters [@wang2026large; @angelopoulos2023prediction\; AAE] or optimally reweight ensembles of candidate prompts, personas, and model checkpoints [@leng2026reducing\; HuMCal].
Complementing these post-inference methods, we align predictions inside the model before inference through both output architecture and training supervision.

Architecturally, several studies avoid the cost and sampling variance of repeated Monte Carlo text generation by extracting next-token probabilities over option symbols (e.g., A, B, and C) from causal LLMs [@kadavath2022language; @kuribayashi-etal-2024-psychometric; @bentegeac2025token; @wadi2026every].
Yet symbol-level readouts remain sensitive to vocabulary and token-frequency priors.
Decision models, also known as System One architectures, resolve this sensitivity via a single-pass scoring head [@palmer2026kev; @deusser2026evaluatingbenchmarkingmodeljev; @geuter2026releasinginnerjevsimple; @li2026llmasjevllmsjevstyledecision; @asseri2026calibratedwhompersonalanguage; @li2026kitescalingjevpopulation].
This head evaluates each supplied option directly in representation space and restricts probability mass strictly to the valid options without open-ended generation or safety refusals.
Crucially for econometric training, outputting exact choice probabilities in a single forward pass makes linear regression operators over experimental designs directly differentiable with respect to model parameters.
However, existing decision models are pretrained on single-label objective benchmarks such as mathematics, code verification, and factual question answering, causing severe probability miscalibration on subjective choice tasks [@gao2026choicesfewerdecisionsordinalscale].

On the training dimension, existing fine-tuning approaches for silicon sampling require access to unreleased response data.
At the token level, @wang2026large fine-tuned GPT-4o on 50 target-study conjoint tasks under a generic persona to emit a single choice letter, finding that small-sample single-token supervision worsened standalone parameter error relative to the human benchmark.
Recent studies improve calibration by supervising causal language models or decision heads on large-scale survey microdata and subgroup response histograms [@suh-etal-2025-language; @huang-etal-2026-distribution; @ku2026siliconsamplingcrosssurveytransfer].
When respondent-level choice microdata is available, minimizing CE on a probabilistic decision head effectively calibrates conditional choice probabilities across personas.
Yet across conjoint analysis, discrete-choice modeling [@mcfadden1972conditional; @train2009discrete], and randomized online or field trials, published articles and archival industry reports rarely disclose raw respondent choices, reporting instead experimental designs and estimated regression tables.
We bridge this data gap by supervising decision models directly on published population OLS coefficients via an unbiased split-sample moment loss, deployed either standalone with a base-distribution KL anchor when no microdata exists or jointly alongside respondent-level CE when augmenting in-house microdata with external literature tables.

# Methodology {#sec-methodology}

**Decision model architecture and choice probabilities.**
Consider an experimental or survey study consisting of $N$ discrete-choice tasks indexed by $t \in \{1, \dots, N\}$.
Each task $t$ pairs a respondent's multi-attribute persona state $\mathbf{s}_t$ (e.g., sex, age, education, income, political party, and race) with a question stem presenting $K_t$ discrete answer options $\{1, \dots, K_t\}$.
When individual choice microdata is available, let $\mathbf{y}_t = (y_{t,1}, \dots, y_{t,K_t})^\top \in \{0, 1\}^{K_t}$ denote the observed one-hot choice vector on task $t$, where $y_{t,k} = 1$ if the respondent selected option $k$ and $0$ otherwise.

Given persona state $\mathbf{s}_t$, a single-pass decision model [@palmer2026kev] scores all $K_t$ options in one causal forward pass without a vocabulary generation head.
The prompt places $\mathbf{s}_t$ in a state segment, followed by the question stem, each option $k$ enclosed in dedicated option delimiters, and a terminal decision token appended after the final option.
Because the terminal decision token follows all $K_t$ options, its final-layer hidden state $\mathbf{h}^{\mathrm{dec}}_t(\mathbf{s}_t) \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}}$ causally attends to the persona, the question stem, and the full option set.
Let $\mathbf{h}_{t,k}(\mathbf{s}_t) \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{model}}}$ denote the final-layer hidden state at the closing delimiter of option $k$.
Using learned affine projections $(\mathbf{W}_q, \mathbf{b}_q)$ and $(\mathbf{W}_k, \mathbf{b}_k)$ with $\mathbf{W}_q, \mathbf{W}_k \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{head}} \times d_{\mathrm{model}}}$ and $\mathbf{b}_q, \mathbf{b}_k \in \mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{head}}}$, the decision head computes a scalar score $z_{t,k}(\mathbf{s}_t; \theta)$ for each option $k$:
$$
z_{t,k}(\mathbf{s}_t; \theta) = \frac{\big(\mathbf{W}_q \mathbf{h}^{\mathrm{dec}}_t(\mathbf{s}_t) + \mathbf{b}_q\big)^\top \big(\mathbf{W}_k \mathbf{h}_{t,k}(\mathbf{s}_t) + \mathbf{b}_k\big)}{\sqrt{d_{\mathrm{head}}}}.
$$ {#eq-pointer-head}
Applying a softmax function yields the normalized choice probability vector $\mathbf{p}_t(\theta) = (p_{t,1}(\theta), \dots, p_{t,K_t}(\theta))^\top$ in a single pass:
$$
p_{t,k}(\theta) = P_{\mathrm{model}}(Y_t = k \mid \mathbf{s}_t; \theta) = \frac{\exp\!\big(z_{t,k}(\mathbf{s}_t; \theta)\big)}{\sum_{m=1}^{K_t} \exp\!\big(z_{t,m}(\mathbf{s}_t; \theta)\big)}.
$$ {#eq-model-pmf}
When respondent choices $\mathbf{y}_t$ are observed, model parameters $\theta$ can be supervised directly via mini-batch cross-entropy over a sampled task batch $S \subset \{1, \dots, N\}$:
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(\theta; S) = -\frac{1}{|S|} \sum_{t \in S} \sum_{k=1}^{K_t} y_{t,k} \log p_{t,k}(\theta).
$$ {#eq-resp-ce}

**Population OLS operators and published targets.**
Concatenating option probabilities across all $N$ tasks in a study yields the flat vector $\mathbf{p}(\theta) = (\mathbf{p}_1(\theta)^\top, \dots, \mathbf{p}_N(\theta)^\top)^\top \in [0, 1]^M$, where $M = \sum_{t=1}^N K_t$, with corresponding stacked human choices $\mathbf{y} \in \{0, 1\}^M$.
Any linear econometric specification estimated on the study can be written over $R$ regression rows via a full-column-rank design matrix $\mathbf{X} \in \mathbb{R}^{R \times c}$ (comprising an intercept, any nuisance controls, and $d$ focal treatment columns indexed by $\mathcal{T} \subset \{1, \dots, c\}$) and a fixed sparse weight matrix $\mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{R \times M}$ that maps option probabilities to regression outcomes $\mathbf{W}\mathbf{p}(\theta) \in \mathbb{R}^R$ (e.g., selecting each displayed profile's choice probability in conjoint average marginal component effects or the healthier item's choice probability in a randomized trial).
For training, dividing by the human outcome standard deviation $\sigma > 0$ places coefficients across studies on a common dimensionless scale.
Using the Moore-Penrose pseudoinverse $\mathbf{X}^\dagger = (\mathbf{X}^\top \mathbf{X})^{-1}\mathbf{X}^\top$, define the fixed standardized population slope operator:
$$
\mathbf{B} = \frac{1}{\sigma} \big(\mathbf{X}^\dagger\big)_{\mathcal{T}, :} \mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times M},
$$ {#eq-pop-operator}
partitioned by task into column blocks $\mathbf{B} = [\mathbf{B}_1, \dots, \mathbf{B}_N]$ with $\mathbf{B}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times K_t}$.
Under @eq-pop-operator, the model's standardized population OLS slopes are an exact linear map of its single-pass probabilities, $\boldsymbol{\beta}(\theta) = \mathbf{B}\mathbf{p}(\theta) = \sum_{t=1}^N \mathbf{B}_t \mathbf{p}_t(\theta)$, and a published regression table supplies the standardized human target $\boldsymbol{\beta}^* \in \mathbb{R}^d$ (which equals $\mathbf{B}\mathbf{y}$ without requiring individual choices $\mathbf{y}$).
When a study estimates $G > 1$ regressions, we construct $(\mathbf{B}^{(g)}, \boldsymbol{\beta}^{*(g)})$ for each $g \in \{1, \dots, G\}$ and average the resulting regression losses equally across $g$.

**Unbiased split-sample population-beta loss.**
To align model-implied slopes $\boldsymbol{\beta}(\theta)$ with a published table $\boldsymbol{\beta}^*$, our target population objective is the standardized slope MSE:
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pop}}(\theta) = \frac{1}{d} \left\lVert \mathbf{B}\mathbf{p}(\theta) - \boldsymbol{\beta}^* \right\rVert_2^2.
$$ {#eq-pop-mse}
Evaluating @eq-pop-mse directly per optimization step is intractable because $\mathbf{B}\mathbf{p}(\theta)$ sums over all $N$ tasks whereas stochastic gradient descent evaluates a mini-batch $S$ of $|S| \ll N$ tasks.
Naive mini-batch surrogates fail for two reasons.
Refitting OLS inside a small batch $S$ requires unreleased choices $\mathbf{y}_t$ and squares ill-conditioned small-sample design inverses, whereas substituting a single-batch estimate $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_S(\theta)$ into $\frac{1}{d}\lVert \hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_S(\theta) - \boldsymbol{\beta}^* \rVert_2^2$ adds positive variance bias $\frac{1}{d}\mathrm{tr}\,\mathrm{Cov}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_S(\theta))$, which increases with across-persona heterogeneity in $\mathbf{p}_t(\theta)$ and penalizes the model for conditioning on respondent personas.

To construct an unbiased, low-variance gradient estimator without respondent choices or stale cached predictions, we run a single no-gradient evaluation pass at initialization $\theta_0$ to record frozen base probabilities $\mathbf{p}_0 = \mathbf{p}(\theta_0)$ and base slopes $\boldsymbol{\beta}_0 = \mathbf{B}\mathbf{p}_0$.
Rewriting $\boldsymbol{\beta}(\theta) = \boldsymbol{\beta}_0 + \sum_{t=1}^N \mathbf{B}_t (\mathbf{p}_t(\theta) - \mathbf{p}_{0,t})$, any uniform subsample $S_m \subset \{1, \dots, N\}$ yields an exact control-variate estimator of the current population slopes:
$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_m(\theta) = \boldsymbol{\beta}_0 + \frac{N}{|S_m|} \sum_{t \in S_m} \mathbf{B}_t \big(\mathbf{p}_t(\theta) - \mathbf{p}_{0,t}\big).
$$ {#eq-cv-beta}
Because $\mathbf{p}_0$ is fixed, $\mathbf{p}_{0,t}$ cancels in expectation at every step so $\mathbb{E}_{S_m}[\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_m(\theta)] = \boldsymbol{\beta}(\theta)$ without staleness bias, while subtracting $\mathbf{p}_{0,t}$ reduces mini-batch variance.
Partitioning each shuffled batch $S$ ($|S| \ge 2$) into two disjoint halves $S_1$ and $S_2$ of sizes $\lfloor |S| / 2 \rfloor$ and $\lceil |S| / 2 \rceil$, we define the split-sample cross loss as the inner product of their estimation errors:
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\beta\text{-cross}}(\theta; S_1, S_2) = \frac{1}{d} \big(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_1(\theta) - \boldsymbol{\beta}^*\big)^\top \big(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_2(\theta) - \boldsymbol{\beta}^*\big).
$$ {#eq-cross-loss}
Up to negligible $\mathcal{O}(1/N)$ finite-population sampling covariance without replacement, $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_1(\theta)$ and $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_2(\theta)$ are independent unbiased estimators of $\boldsymbol{\beta}(\theta)$, implying $\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{L}_{\beta\text{-cross}}(\theta; S_1, S_2)] = \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pop}}(\theta)$ and $\mathbb{E}[\nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\beta\text{-cross}}(\theta; S_1, S_2)] = \nabla_\theta \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pop}}(\theta)$ (individual step realizations of @eq-cross-loss may be negative).

**KL anchoring across training regimes.**
Because $d \ll M$, minimizing @eq-cross-loss alone constrains only $d$ linear projections of $\mathbf{p}(\theta)$ and leaves the $(M - d)$-dimensional nullspace $\ker(\mathbf{B})$ unconstrained.
Without regularization along those unconstrained directions, prolonged optimization can sharpen option logits and push task probabilities toward zero or one while still maintaining $\mathbf{B}\mathbf{p}(\theta) \approx \boldsymbol{\beta}^*$, distorting choice uncertainty and destabilizing out-of-sample treatment-effect estimates.
To stabilize table supervision without using any respondent choices, we anchor predicted probabilities on table-study tasks to the frozen base distribution $\mathbf{p}_{0,t}$ through a forward Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence penalty:
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta; S) = \frac{1}{|S|} \sum_{t \in S} \sum_{k=1}^{K_t} p_{0,t,k} \log \frac{p_{0,t,k}}{p_{t,k}(\theta)}.
$$ {#eq-kl-anchor}
Combining @eq-cross-loss and @eq-kl-anchor with slope weight $\lambda > 0$ and anchor weight $\alpha \ge 0$ yields the table-study objective:
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{table}}(\theta; S) = \lambda \, \mathcal{L}_{\beta\text{-cross}}(\theta; S_1, S_2) + \alpha \, \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta; S).
$$ {#eq-table-loss}
Evaluating @eq-kl-anchor requires zero additional forward passes because $\mathbf{p}_{0,t}$ is already stored in memory for @eq-cv-beta.
Furthermore, $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta; S)$ is convex in the option logits with per-task logit gradient $\mathbf{p}_t(\theta) - \mathbf{p}_{0,t}$, which smoothly pulls drifting probabilities back toward $\mathbf{p}_{0,t}$ and prevents collapse onto zero or one.

In the table-only regime, where no microdata is available for any study, we minimize @eq-table-loss directly over mini-batches drawn from the table study.
In the hybrid regime, where in-house choice microdata $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{micro}}$ is paired with external table-only studies $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{table}}$, we interleave single-study mini-batches across both sources and minimize respondent-level CE on $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{micro}}$ alongside the same anchored table loss @eq-table-loss on $\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{table}}$:
$$
\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{hybrid}}(\theta; S) = \mathbb{I}(S \subset \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{micro}}) \, \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}(\theta; S) + \mathbb{I}(S \subset \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{table}}) \, \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{table}}(\theta; S).
$$ {#eq-hybrid-loss}
Under @eq-hybrid-loss, $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{CE}}$ calibrates choice uncertainty on the microdata domain, $\mathcal{L}_{\beta\text{-cross}}$ transfers missing attribute trade-offs from external regression tables, and the KL anchor directly regularizes the unconstrained nullspace of the external table study's tasks while keeping table supervision uniform across regimes.
Setting $\alpha = 0$ removes the KL anchor in either regime, enabling a direct ablation of whether the anchor is needed when training on a table alone or alongside microdata.

# Experimental setup {#sec-setup}

**Studies and split roles.**
We evaluate the framework across five published US choice studies spanning distinct domains with no domain overlap between training and evaluation (@tbl-datasets).
Two studies serve as training data.
The first, `Electricity` [@wu2025partisan\; 1,861 respondents, 18,591 choices], is a paired electricity-plan conjoint experiment varying monthly bill (`$105` to `$125`), renewable-energy share (`10%` to `100%`), and local renewable production (`No` or `Yes`), yielding $d = 8$ OLS average marginal component effects (AMCEs).
Because @wu2025partisan displays these eight AMCEs graphically in Figure 3 rather than in a printed numerical table, we reproduce the eight slopes using the study's published OLS specification and divide by the outcome standard deviation $\sigma$ to stand in for a published regression table; in table-supervised regimes, all 18,591 respondent choices are strictly withheld from the loss and gradients.
The second training study, `Drones` [@berke2023drone\; 3,625 respondents, 36,297 choices], is a discrete-choice experiment on drone versus ground delivery across four vendor contexts varying delivery fee (`$0` to `$10`), wait time, and drone privacy, with no sustainability attribute.
In our design, `Drones` represents in-house respondent microdata and enters training only through @eq-resp-ce.

Three unseen studies serve as out-of-domain benchmarks separated by both split role and attribute overlap with training (@tbl-datasets).
`Flights` [@goldfarb2026comfort\; 1,000 respondents, 5,000 choices, 12 OLS AMCEs] is a paired airline-ticket conjoint experiment varying ticket price (`$250` to `$325`), sustainable aviation fuel, airline, baggage, legroom, and seat selection.
We designate `Flights` as the shared-attribute validation set, using it to select every training run's checkpoint and to judge the KL-anchor ablation so that held-out test sets never inform modeling choices.
`Flights` therefore differs from the held-out test sets both because it selects checkpoints and because it shares the core price-versus-sustainability trade-off with `Electricity` (and small delivery fees with `Drones`), alongside four flight-specific attributes.
The two strictly held-out zero-shot benchmarks are disjoint-attribute tests whose attributes have no overlap with training: `Food labels` [@grummon2025nutrition\; 5,633 respondents, 33,798 choices, 5 OLS arm contrasts], a six-arm front-of-package nutrition-labeling randomized trial measuring healthier-product identification relative to the positive-label control, and `Vaccines` [@kreps2020factors\; 1,971 respondents, 9,855 choices, 11 OLS AMCEs], a three-option COVID-19 vaccine conjoint experiment (two vaccine profiles plus an opt-out option) varying efficacy, duration, side effects, FDA authorization, country of origin, and endorsements.
Neither `Food labels` nor `Vaccines` is used during training, hyperparameter tuning, or checkpoint selection, and neither includes price or sustainability attributes.

**Data-access regimes.**
Across every model scale, we compare six main regimes spanning the data-access ladder.
`Untrained` evaluates the off-the-shelf decision model without fine-tuning ($0$ steps).
`Electricity (OLS slopes)` trains solely on the eight @wu2025partisan OLS slopes using the anchored table objective @eq-table-loss ($\lambda = 1.0$, $\alpha = 0.005$, 1,395 steps over $3$ epochs) without using respondent choices, whereas `Electricity (microdata)` trains via @eq-resp-ce on all 18,591 @wu2025partisan choices (1,395 steps) to provide a matched within-study microdata reference.
`Drones (microdata)` trains via @eq-resp-ce on the 36,297 @berke2023drone choices (2,730 steps), representing a researcher's proprietary microdata baseline.
`Drones (microdata) + Electricity (OLS slopes)` applies the anchored hybrid objective @eq-hybrid-loss ($\lambda = 1.0$, $\alpha = 0.005$, 4,125 steps) to combine in-house `Drones` microdata with external `Electricity` OLS slopes, and `Drones + Electricity (microdata)` pools respondent choices across both training studies under @eq-resp-ce (4,125 steps) as a full-microdata reference.
To isolate the effect of KL anchoring, we additionally run unanchored counterparts ($\alpha = 0$) of both `Electricity (OLS slopes)` and `Drones (microdata) + Electricity (OLS slopes)` under identical optimization settings, together with a sensitivity sweep over $\alpha$ on `Electricity (OLS slopes)`, evaluated strictly on the `Flights` validation set.

**Models, optimization, and evaluation metrics.**
We evaluate the open-weight `KEV` decision-model family [@palmer2026kev; @gao2026choicesfewerdecisionsordinalscale] across three scales (`KEV-0.8B`, `KEV-4B`, and `KEV-9B`).
Each base checkpoint is loaded in `bfloat16` precision and adapted with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA, rank $r = 64$, scaling $\alpha_{\mathrm{LoRA}} = 128$, dropout $0.05$) across all linear backbone projections alongside the trainable decision head.
All fine-tuned regimes use identical optimization settings across model scales: AdamW with a peak learning rate of $5 \times 10^{-6}$, a OneCycle learning-rate schedule with a $10\%$ warmup and cosine decay, weight decay $0.01$, gradient-norm clipping at $1.0$, mini-batch size $|S| = 40$ tasks, random seed $42$, and $3$ epochs.
Within each epoch, tasks are partitioned into single-study mini-batches (and, for `Drones`, single-vendor mini-batches) of $40$ tasks and interleaved in shuffled order, merging any one-task remainder on a table study into another batch so every split cross-loss step satisfies $|S| \ge 2$.
To compute exact gradients of @eq-table-loss within GPU memory limits, each table-study step uses a two-pass micro-chunked procedure (a first no-gradient pass collects option logits across micro-chunks to evaluate @eq-table-loss and its logit gradients, and a second pass replays identical dropout states to backpropagate those gradients), whereas microdata steps accumulate exact additive cross-entropy gradients in a single pass.

Every run is validated on `Flights` every $32$ optimization steps ($1,280$ training tasks), as well as at step $0$ and the final step, and the checkpoint attaining the lowest validation population slope MSE is selected for test evaluation.
Whereas training standardizes table targets by $\sigma$ in @eq-pop-operator and @eq-pop-mse, all validation and held-out test metrics compare unstandardized population OLS slopes $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}(\theta) = (\mathbf{X}^\dagger)_{\mathcal{T},:}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{p}(\theta)$ against the corresponding human OLS slopes $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\mathrm{human}} = (\mathbf{X}^\dagger)_{\mathcal{T},:}\mathbf{W}\mathbf{y}$ in each study's native probability-point units.
Our primary metric across all benchmarks is unstandardized population slope MSE, $\frac{1}{d}\lVert \tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}(\theta) - \tilde{\boldsymbol{\beta}}^{\mathrm{human}} \rVert_2^2$ (reported multiplied by $10^3$).
As a secondary individual-level diagnostic reported in the Web Appendix, we compute choice-distribution KL divergence (Choice KL), defined as the mean negative natural log probability $-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{t=1}^N \sum_{k=1}^{K_t} y_{t,k} \log p_{t,k}(\theta)$ in nats across all tasks in a study.

# Study 1: Choice-Based Conjoint Analysis {#sec-study1}

To test whether fine-tuning on human response distributions generalizes to out-of-sample human studies, we estimate each held-out study's econometric model on the predicted responses and compare the resulting regression parameters against the human estimates.

## Experimental Design and Multinomial Logit Specification

For our first held-out study, following the benchmark protocol of @wang2026large, we use a COVID-19 vaccine conjoint dataset [@kreps2020factors], summarized in @tbl-datasets, to investigate part-worth utility recovery.
In this study, 1,971 US respondents each complete $t \in \{1, \dots, 5\}$ paired choice tasks (9,855 observations).
Each task presents two hypothetical vaccine profiles (`Option A` and `Option B`) with binary attribute vectors $\mathbf{x}_{i,t,A}, \mathbf{x}_{i,t,B} \in \{0, 1\}^d$, alongside a no-vaccine outside option (`Option C`) whose utility is normalized to zero.
Profiles vary across $7$ attributes coded as $d = 11$ non-reference binary indicators (@apptbl-wang-coefs).

Under the standard Multinomial Logit (MNL) model [@wang2026large], choice probabilities for parameter vector $\boldsymbol{\beta} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ are:
$$
P_m(\mathbf{x}_{i,t}; \boldsymbol{\beta}) = \frac{\exp(\mathbf{x}_{i,t,m}^\top \boldsymbol{\beta})}{1 + \exp(\mathbf{x}_{i,t,A}^\top \boldsymbol{\beta}) + \exp(\mathbf{x}_{i,t,B}^\top \boldsymbol{\beta})}, \qquad m \in \{A, B\},
$$ {#eq-mnl-probs}
with $P_C(\mathbf{x}_{i,t}; \boldsymbol{\beta}) = 1 - P_A(\mathbf{x}_{i,t}; \boldsymbol{\beta}) - P_B(\mathbf{x}_{i,t}; \boldsymbol{\beta})$.
Given observed or predicted choice shares $(p_{i,t,A}, p_{i,t,B}, p_{i,t,C})$ across $n$ choice sets, we estimate $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}$ via Newton-CG maximum likelihood:
$$
\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta} \in \mathbb{R}^d} -\frac{1}{n} \sum_{(i,t)} \sum_{m \in \{A, B, C\}} p_{i,t,m} \log P_m(\mathbf{x}_{i,t}; \boldsymbol{\beta}).
$$ {#eq-mnl-mle}
Human respondents and generative LLMs supply one-hot choices, whereas decision models supply continuous probabilities from @eq-model-pmf.
Let $\boldsymbol{\beta}^* \in \mathbb{R}^{11}$ denote the ground-truth MNL vector estimated on all 9,855 human choices.
Following @wang2026large, we evaluate models on a 200-respondent subsample (*n* = 1,000 choice sets) using Mean Absolute Percentage Error ($\mathrm{MAPE}$) and Mean Squared Error ($\mathrm{MSE}$):
$$
\mathrm{MAPE}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}, \boldsymbol{\beta}^*) = \frac{1}{d} \sum_{j=1}^{d} \frac{|\hat{\beta}_j - \beta^*_j|}{|\beta^*_j|} \times 100\%,
$$ {#eq-wang-mape}
$$
\mathrm{MSE}(\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}, \boldsymbol{\beta}^*) = \frac{1}{d} \sum_{j=1}^{d} (\hat{\beta}_j - \beta^*_j)^2.
$$ {#eq-wang-mse}

We test both unconditioned random personas and $9$-attribute respondent personas (US region, gender, age, education, race, income, religion, political party, and ideology; @apptbl-attributes).
Decision models score the verbatim survey instrument [@kreps2020factors], whereas generative LLMs (`Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite` at `minimal` and `high` thinking; `Gemini 4 Argon` at `low` and `high` thinking) use the @wang2026large prompt format (which additionally states country).
Unlike @wang2026large, who excluded vaccine opt-out respondents due to LLM safety refusals, we retain the full untruncated respondent population and benchmark against MNL estimated directly on the 200 sampled humans.

## Conjoint Estimation Results

**Generative LLM bias.**
Estimating MNL on the 200 sampled humans yields a finite-sample benchmark of $\mathrm{MSE} = 0.0065$ (@tbl-wang-mnl; @appfig-wang-random and @appfig-wang-persona).
Consistent with @wang2026large, generative LLMs exhibit severe bias under random personas ($\mathrm{MSE} = 3.2073$ to $26.2179$).
Conditioning on the $9$ respondent attributes cuts error substantially ($\mathrm{MSE} = 0.5925$ to $2.1687$), yet estimates remain far from the human benchmark.
Moreover, higher reasoning budgets and model scale worsen parameter recovery.
Under respondent personas, raising `Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite` thinking from `minimal` to `high` doubles MSE ($0.5925$ to $1.1984$), while `Gemini 4 Argon` degrades further ($1.7637$ at `low` and $2.1687$ at `high`).

**Why choice probabilities matter.**
Generative LLMs bias conjoint estimation because discrete text generation collapses choice uncertainty and triggers safety refusals.
Under random personas, generative LLMs rarely select the no-vaccine option ($0.0\%$ to $3.0\%$ vs. $20.3\%$ for humans), while `Gemini 4 Argon (high)` refuses $16$ of $1,000$ tasks.
Even under respondent personas, near-deterministic profile selection pushes conditional choice shares toward zero or one, causing severe MNL scale inflation (@fig-wang-coefs, Panel B; @apptbl-wang-coefs): `Efficacy: 90%` reaches $+1.846$ to $+3.538$ versus $+0.746$ for humans.
Scoring options directly via `Kev 9B (base)` ($T = 2.19$) eliminates refusals and cuts MSE by an order of magnitude ($0.2449$ random; $0.0815$ respondent).
Collapsing those same `Kev 9B (base)` probabilities into one-hot top choices inflates respondent-persona MSE nearly $23$-fold ($0.0815$ to $1.8678$), showing that continuous probability readouts--rather than discrete choices--are essential to prevent scale distortion.

**Distributional survey fine-tuning.**
Evaluated zero-shot--without training or calibration on conjoint data--`Kev 9B (FT)` reduces MNL MSE relative to `Kev 9B (base)` by $64.3\%$ under random personas ($0.2449$ to $0.0875$) and by $67.2\%$ under respondent personas ($0.0815$ to $0.0267$; @tbl-wang-mnl).
Fine-tuning also lowers choice cross-entropy (`1.6370` to `1.5192` bits under random personas; `1.5255` to `1.4449` bits under respondent personas) and raises predicted no-vaccine shares ($19.0\%$ and $28.1\%$, up from $11.9\%$ and $16.4\%$ for `Kev 9B (base)`).
At the attribute level (@fig-wang-coefs, Panel A; @apptbl-wang-coefs), `Kev 9B (base)` overestimates the part-worths of vaccine efficacy and institutional endorsements, with only $5$ of $11$ estimates falling within the human subsample's $95\%$ confidence intervals.
By contrast, `Kev 9B (FT)` recovers $8$ of $11$ estimates within those $95\%$ confidence intervals, closely aligning with full-sample human part-worths on efficacy, FDA Emergency Use Authorization, country of origin, and endorsements while attenuating protection duration and rare major side effects toward zero.

# Study 2: Front-of-Package Nutrition Labeling Trial {#sec-study2}

## Experimental Design and OLS Specification

Our second held-out study evaluates causal treatment-effect recovery in a front-of-package nutrition labeling trial [@grummon2025nutrition].
In this experiment, *N* = 5,633 US grocery shoppers are randomized to one of six between-subjects labeling arms (`Positive` serves as the reference arm; @apptbl-grummon2025-coefs).
Each shopper completes $q \in \{1, \dots, 6\}$ three-option product choice tasks across food and beverage categories, where $y_1$ denotes the objectively healthier option.

For each shopper $i$, we compute the mean probability of selecting the healthier product across the six tasks, $\bar{p}_i = \frac{1}{6} \sum_{q=1}^6 p_{i,q,1}$, where $p_{i,q,1}$ is the binary choice indicator $y_{i,q,1}$ for human shoppers and the predicted probability $P_{\mathrm{model}}(Y_{i,q} = y_1 \mid \mathbf{s}_i; \theta)$ under the assigned arm for decision models.
Following @grummon2025nutrition, we regress $\bar{p}_i$ on the five treatment-arm indicators via ordinary least squares (OLS) with HC1 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors to obtain $\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}} \in \mathbb{R}^5$ relative to `Positive`.
We evaluate models on a 200-shopper subsample (*n* = 1,200 choices) against the full-sample human vector $\boldsymbol{\beta}^*$ (*N* = 5,633).
Each shopper profile contains $13$ attributes (@apptbl-attributes): $6$ demographic attributes seen in survey training (sex, age, education, income, race, and household size) and $7$ covariates completely unseen during training (Hispanic ethnicity, number of children, SNAP receipt, WIC receipt, Nutrition Facts label usage, online grocery share, and nutrition literacy score).

## Trial Estimation and Attribute Generalization Results

**Treatment-effect recovery.**
Under $13$-attribute shopper personas, scaling off-the-shelf models from `0.8B` to `9B` worsens choice cross-entropy (`1.4770` to `1.5405` bits; @tbl-grummon2025-ols) and yields higher OLS MSE than unconditioned random prompts at every scale (@appfig-grummon2025-random; @appfig-grummon2025-persona).
Survey fine-tuning reverses this scaling pattern, steadily lowering cross-entropy from `1.5536` bits (`0.8B`) to `1.3479` bits (`9B`).
Whereas smaller fine-tuned models (`0.8B` and `4B`) improve arm rank ordering or MAPE without reducing OLS MSE, `Kev 9B (FT)` improves every metric. 
It reaches a Spearman rank correlation of $\rho = +0.90$, lowers respondent-persona MAPE from $63.7\%$ to $44.3\%$, and reduces OLS MSE by $53.2\%$ ($0.0047$ to $0.0022$; and by $44.1\%$ to $0.0019$ under random prompts), approaching the 200-shopper human benchmark ($\mathrm{MSE} = 0.0016$, $\mathrm{MAPE} = 22.7\%$).
At the arm level (@fig-grummon2025-coefs, Panel A; @apptbl-grummon2025-coefs), `Kev 9B (FT)` places all five estimates within the human subsample's $95\%$ confidence intervals, closely matching full-sample effects on the three symmetrical interpretive labels (`Nutrition Info`, `Positive + Nutrition Info`, and `Spectrum`).
Remaining error concentrates in the two asymmetric `High In` arms, where graphical warning shields in @grummon2025nutrition were serialized into text without visual warning cues.

**Generalization to unseen shopper attributes.**
To test whether fine-tuning merely memorizes training-corpus demographics, we evaluate each model when prompted with one shopper attribute at a time across the $6$ seen demographics and the $7$ unseen covariates (@fig-grummon2025-coefs, Panel B; @apptbl-grummon2025-personas).
Across individual attributes, off-the-shelf `Kev 9B (base)` varies widely in cross-entropy (`1.3935` to `1.6661` bits) and performs worse than uniform guessing (`1.5850` bits) on `Nutrition Facts label usage` (`1.6661`) and `Share of groceries bought online` (`1.6016`).
If survey fine-tuning memorized only in-corpus demographics, improvements would be confined to the $6$ seen attributes.
Instead, `Kev 9B (FT)` lowers cross-entropy on every attribute, converging to virtually identical mean cross-entropy on the $7$ unseen covariates (`1.3473` bits, vs. `1.5328` for `Kev 9B (base)`) and the $6$ seen demographics (`1.3477` bits, vs. `1.4866` for `Kev 9B (base)`).

| Estimator | CE (bits) | MAPE (%) | MSE | Spearman $\rho$ |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Human subsample (*N* = 200, *n* = 1,200) | — | 22.7% | 0.0016 | +0.40 |
| Kev 0.8B (base) | 1.4770 | 58.5% | 0.0074 | +0.50 |
| Kev 0.8B (FT) | 1.5536 | 66.5% | 0.0078 | +0.70 |
| Kev 4B (base) | 1.5124 | 95.9% | 0.0088 | +0.80 |
| Kev 4B (FT) | 1.4659 | 83.0% | 0.0099 | +0.80 |
| Kev 9B (base) | 1.5405 | 63.7% | 0.0047 | +0.80 |
| Kev 9B (FT) | 1.3479 | 44.3% | 0.0022 | +0.90 |

# Discussion and Conclusion {#sec-discussion}

Our findings show that the severe econometric biases in generative LLM silicon sampling [@goli2024frontiers; @leng2026reducing; @wang2026large] stem from discrete text generation and single-label post-training rather than fundamental limits of foundation models. Whereas recent marketing methods correct fixed LLM outputs after inference using target-study human data [@wang2026large; @leng2026reducing], aligning models before inference requires pairing a probabilistic readout with distributional supervision. Architecturally, single-pass decision heads output normalized probabilities directly over valid options, eliminating free-text parsing errors, Monte Carlo sampling variance, safety refusals on sensitive opt-out choices, and the nearly $23$-fold MNL error inflation caused by discretizing choices. Substantively, minimizing cross-entropy against empirical sample distributions across 1.88 million general survey responses (`US ISSP` and `Twin-2K-500`) calibrates conditional choice probabilities at unit temperature ($T = 1.00$), generalizing zero-shot across unseen respondent covariates and substantially improving conjoint MNL and experimental OLS parameter recovery.

For marketing researchers, distributionally aligned decision models enable fast, deterministic pre-testing before primary data collection (e.g., screening candidate conjoint attributes, auditing survey instruments, or evaluating policy messaging across demographic subgroups in a single forward pass per task). At the same time, zero-shot simulation complements rather than replaces human experimentation for high-stakes managerial or regulatory decisions, as `Kev 9B (FT)` still exhibits higher estimation error than a 200-participant human sample ($\mathrm{MSE} = 0.0267$ vs. $0.0065$ in conjoint MNL; $0.0022$ vs. $0.0016$ in trial OLS). When researchers do collect primary human responses in the target study, upstream distributional alignment and downstream statistical calibration [@wang2026large; @leng2026reducing] are naturally complementary. Passing refusal-free, persona-conditioned probability vectors from `Kev 9B (FT)` into AI-augmented estimators [@wang2026large] or checkpoint ensembles [@leng2026reducing] could inject calibrated respondent-level variation while reducing reliance on large human calibration samples.

Three boundary conditions define priorities for future research. 
First, our nutrition trial highlights a modality boundary of text-only silicon sampling, as serializing graphical `High In` warning shields into text loses visual salience cues. 
Extending distributional training to multimodal vision-language decision heads that score package mockups and advertisements directly is an immediate next step. 
Second, because our training corpus centers on general US social and behavioral attitudes, `Kev 9B (FT)` attenuates unfamiliar clinical attributes (`Duration` and `Major side effects`) toward zero, and smaller models (`0.8B` and `4B`) do not improve OLS MSE. 
Incorporating historical commercial conjoint studies, scanner panels, and cross-national surveys would broaden domain transfer. 
Third, conditioning solely on static persona covariates $\mathbf{s}_i$ treats repeated choices per respondent as conditionally independent, motivating sequential conditioning on prior choices or integration with mixed-logit random-coefficients models. 
Together, single-pass decision architectures and distributional survey training provide a practical, extensible foundation for behavioral simulation in marketing science.
